title: The Candidates Who Made History in the Midterms
author: Chad de Guzman
body:
The 2026 U.S. elections have already made history in a number of ways.

Even before any vote was cast, it was the most expensive election cycle in U.S. history in terms of political ad spending, with more than $11 billion expected to be spent, according to analysis firm AdImpact. States had redrawn congressional maps between censuses at a rate the National Conference of State Legislatures says has not been seen since the 1800s, as parties try to secure victories. And Donald Trump had a historically low approval rating for a President heading into the midterms.

This election was already set to see massive turnover on Capitol Hill, with dozens of members of Congress resigning, retiring, or seeking other office. The so-called blue wave of Democratic victories in the House and Senate will also see even more Republican incumbents ousted.

Several identity barriers have also been broken, including the election of the first openly gay male U.S. Senator, the first Black woman governor, and the first Native American female governor. A handful of other races could see even more national historic firsts.

Here’s what to know about these historymakers.

Potential first Black Speaker of the House

Rep. Joseph Rainey of South Carolina is believed to be the first Black American elected to the U.S. House in 1870. He also was the first Black American to preside over the House of Representatives—albeit temporarily—during a debate on an appropriations bill providing for the management of Native American reservations in 1874.

But no Black person has served as Speaker of the House. But with Democrats regaining control of the House, that could change: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who won re-election in the uncompetitive race against Republican opponent Lewis Mizrahi, could be the first. Jeffries, who served in Congress for nearly 14 years, was elected unopposed in 2022 as House Democratic Leader, succeeding Speaker Emerita Nancy Pelosi and making him the first Black leader of a major political party in Congress. But even with re-election, the path to the speakership isn’t guaranteed, as the center-left Jeffries may have to unite an ideologically fractious Democratic caucus.

First Muslim Senator

Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a former local public health director and podcaster who has never held elected public office, became the first Muslim U.S. Senator, beating Republican candidate Mike Rogers.

El-Sayed ran on a progressive platform, including advocating for Medicare for All and ending U.S. military funding to Israel, which has ruffled some moderate and Jewish Democrats. His identity has also become a campaign target for Republicans: Rogers and Donald Trump have tried to link El-Sayed and his family to the transnational extremist group Muslim Brotherhood, and El-Sayed has been pressured to reaffirm his commitment to the Constitution over his faith, which defenders have said reflects the Islamophobia he faces.

“I'm not running to be the first Muslim anything,” El-Sayed told CNN in August. “I just want to be a really, really great senator for my state.”

First openly gay male Senator

The first openly LGBT person elected to the U.S. Senate was Sen. Tammy Baldwin (D, Wis.), who was elected in 2012, but Chris Pappas, a Democratic House member who has represented New Hampshire's 1st congressional district since 2019, will become the first out gay man to serve in the U.S. Senate after he defeated Republican nominee John E. Sununu, a former U.S. Senator to fill the seat to be vacated by retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. The 46-year-old Pappas, who married his partner lawyer Vann Bentley in 2023, has been a vocal LGBT rights advocate in Congress.

First Black female governor

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms beat Republican billionaire Rick Jackson in the race to succeed the term-limited Georgia Republican Gov. Brian Kemp.

Bottoms’ victory makes her the state’s first Black and first female governor, as well as the first Black female governor of any state.

Bottoms was the mayor of Atlanta from 2018 to 2022, presiding during the COVID-19 pandemic, and shocked the state’s political establishment when she said she would not seek re-election. She faced criticism from Jackson and others for walking away from the job. She since served in the Biden Administration in various roles, including as a senior adviser and leading the White House Office of Public Engagement.

In Minnesota, Republican gubernatorial candidate Lisa Demuth, who could have shared the historic milestone with Bottoms, lost to Democratic nominee Sen. Amy Klobuchar. Klobuchar broke the state’s glass ceiling, becoming the first woman elected to lead the state.

First Native American female governor

In 2018, Deb Haaland, a member of the Laguna Pueblo, a federally recognized tribe in New Mexico that has existed longer than the U.S. has, made history as one of the first Native American women, alongside Sharice Davids, to be elected to Congress. As a congresswoman, she focused on environmental justice, climate change, and missing and murdered indigenous women. In 2021, Haaland became the Biden Administration’s Interior Secretary.

Now Haaland has made history again, becoming the first Native American woman elected governor of any state. She beat Republican Gregg Hull, the former mayor of Rio Rancho.

Haaland could share this milestone. In Alaska, Bernadette Wilson, who is of Aleut heritage, is a Republican candidate for governor in a race that was too close to call on election night and was rated by forecasters as a toss-up. Wilson, a conservative activist and former radio host, has the backing of President Trump, but veteran Sen. Lisa Murkowski, a moderate Alaska Republican, and her father, former Gov. Frank Murkowski, both endorsed Wilson’s Democratic opponent, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, whom Wilson trailed in the polls.

First Native American female Senators

At least four Native American men have served in the U.S. Senate, but no Native American woman ever has. But that’s set to change after Minnesota’s Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan, a member of the White Earth Band of Ojibwe—the largest federally recognized tribe in Minnesota—beat Republican political newcomer Michele Tafoya.

“I’m not running to make history, but it’s about damn time there was a Native American woman serving in the United States Senate,” Flanagan said on the campaign trail in October. “And she might as well be from White Earth.”

Flanagan could be joined by Alaska’s Mary Peltola. Peltola, a Yup'ik Alaska Native, was first elected to the U.S. House in an August 2022 special election to replace the late Rep. Don Young and became the first Alaska Native member of Congress and the first woman to represent Alaska in the lower chamber. Her tight race for the upper chamber seat against incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, which has been marred by allegations of dirty tricks, was too close to call on election night.
